client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately, like no matter how hard I try, it's never enough. I'm juggling my classes and trying to keep my GPA up, but I also have shifts at the cafe almost every other day just to cover my expenses, and it feels like I'm constantly failing at both. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is just... real, and it doesn't go away just because I talk about it.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting — balancing classes, grades, and work shifts just to stay afloat is a lot, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling stretched so thin. You're right that talking won't make the practical pressures disappear, but sometimes it can help us notice if our mind is adding an extra layer of weight on top of the real ones — like that thought that you're "constantly failing at both." When you say you're failing, what does that actually look like to you — is there specific evidence you're holding onto, or does it feel more like a persistent feeling that's hard to shake?

client: Honestly, it's more of a persistent feeling, but I can point to things too — like last week I left my shift early because I had an exam, and my manager was visibly annoyed, and then I still only got a 71 on the exam. It just felt like proof that no matter what I sacrifice, I'm still not doing well enough at either thing. And that feeling kind of follows me around constantly, like I'm always one bad shift or one bad grade away from everything falling apart.
therapist: That experience with your manager and the exam sounds really discouraging — you made a hard choice, sacrificed something, and it still felt like it wasn't enough, which I can see why would feel like "proof" of failing. But I want to gently notice something: a 71 after leaving a shift early for an exam, while managing this whole balancing act, might actually tell a different story than your mind is framing it. What do you think it would mean if you looked at that same situation as evidence of someone doing their best under genuinely difficult circumstances, rather than evidence of failing?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that framing, but it honestly feels like a stretch. Like, a 71 is still below where I need to be to keep my scholarship, so calling it "doing my best" doesn't change the actual consequences I'm facing. It almost feels like you're trying to make me feel better about something that genuinely has real stakes attached to it.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that, and I don't want to minimize the real stakes — a scholarship threshold is a concrete consequence, not just a feeling, and it deserves to be taken seriously. What I'm not trying to do is talk you out of the reality, but rather make sure the story you're telling yourself about it doesn't add more weight than the situation already carries on its own. So I'm curious — when you imagine everything "falling apart," what does that actually look like, and is there any part of that picture that might have more flexibility or options than it feels like right now?

client: Honestly, when I imagine it falling apart, I picture losing the scholarship, having to tell my parents, and then just... not being able to afford to stay in school at all. Like one bad grade becomes this domino effect where I end up back home feeling like a complete failure. I want to believe there's flexibility somewhere in that picture, but it genuinely feels like every door just closes at once.
therapist: That image of every door closing at once — ending up back home feeling like a failure — sounds like an incredibly heavy thing to be carrying around in the background of every shift and every exam. It makes sense that when the stakes feel that total, even a 71 feels catastrophic. I want to gently ask though: in that domino picture your mind has built, are there any steps along the way where you've actually explored what the options might be — like talking to a financial aid advisor, or understanding what your scholarship actually allows for — or has the fear of the outcome made it hard to look too closely at the details?

client: Honestly, no — I haven't really looked into any of that. Every time I think about calling financial aid or reading through the scholarship terms, I just kind of freeze up and find something else to do, because I think part of me is scared that if I actually look, I'll confirm the worst and there'll be no more "maybe it'll be okay." It's like the not-knowing is terrifying but also the only thing keeping me going right now.
therapist: That makes so much sense — the "maybe" feels like the last bit of breathing room you have, and looking too closely feels like risking losing even that. But what you're describing, that freeze and avoidance, is actually your mind trying to protect you, even though it's also keeping you stuck in this exhausting in-between place where the fear gets to stay as big as it wants to be. Sometimes the imagined worst is actually scarier than the real information — so I'm wondering, if you did make that call and the news wasn't as final as you fear, what do you think that would feel like?

client: I guess... if the news wasn't as bad as I'm imagining, I'd probably feel relieved for like five minutes and then immediately start worrying about whatever comes next. It's hard to even let myself picture that because it almost feels like setting myself up, you know? Like if I let myself hope and then it IS bad, I'll have made it worse somehow by daring to imagine otherwise.
therapist: That belief — that hoping makes a bad outcome hurt more, so it's safer not to hope — is such a common and understandable way the mind tries to protect us, but it also means you're essentially pre-punishing yourself to avoid future pain, which keeps you in a low hum of dread all the time. It's worth noticing that whether the news is good or bad, it will be what it is regardless of whether you let yourself hope beforehand — hope doesn't actually change the outcome, it just changes how you feel in the waiting. I'm curious, has there been a time in your life where you let yourself hope for something and it didn't work out — and did the hoping actually make it worse, or is that more of a story your mind has built up as a rule to live by?

client: I mean... yeah, there was a time I let myself get really excited about a job I interviewed for, told a few people about it, started mentally planning what my life would look like, and then I didn't get it. And honestly, the embarrassment of having told people felt worse than the rejection itself, so in my head that kind of became proof that hoping out loud is dangerous. But I guess when I actually sit with what you're saying... I'm not totally sure the hoping made the disappointment itself worse, it was more the social part that stung.
therapist: That's actually a really important distinction you just made — the hoping itself didn't make the loss worse, it was the vulnerability of having shared it publicly that stung, which is a different thing entirely. Your mind kind of merged those two experiences into one rule, "hoping is dangerous," when really the lesson might be more nuanced, like "I get to be selective about when and with whom I share things while they're still uncertain." What do you think it might feel like to let yourself quietly hope about something — just for yourself, without telling anyone — and whether that still feels as risky?

client: That's... actually kind of an interesting way to put it, and I hadn't separated those two things before. But I think even hoping quietly still scares me, because if it doesn't work out, I'm still left alone with that disappointment and no one even knows to check on me. It's like the loneliness of a private hope failing might actually feel worse in some ways.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just shared — this fear that if you hope privately and it falls apart, you'll be sitting alone with that pain and invisible to everyone around you. That tells me something important, which is that underneath all the stress about grades and money, there might also be a loneliness piece here, a feeling of going through something really hard without enough support around you. I'm wondering — is there anyone in your life right now, even one person, who you feel like could handle knowing what you're actually going through?

client: I mean... maybe my roommate, kind of? But I don't know, she has her own stuff going on, and I feel like if I start unloading on her she'll either think I'm being dramatic or she'll worry about me and then I'll feel guilty for stressing her out. It's like even thinking about telling someone feels like it creates more problems than it solves.
therapist: It's really telling that even in the moment of naming someone who might be there for you, your mind immediately jumps to protecting her from you — that's a pattern worth noticing, where your needs feel like a burden before you've even given anyone the chance to show up. The thought that she'll find you dramatic or that you'll stress her out are predictions, not facts, and they might say more about how you've learned to shrink yourself than about how your roommate would actually respond. What do you think that belief — that your struggles are too much for the people around you — has cost you over time?

client: That question kind of hits harder than I expected, honestly. I think it's cost me a lot — like, I've just gotten used to handling everything alone, and somewhere along the way that became my whole identity, the person who doesn't need anything from anyone. But it's also lonely in a way I don't really let myself think about too much, because if I do, I have to admit how much I've been missing out on.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to admit — that "person who doesn't need anything" identity probably kept you safe and functional for a long time, but it sounds like it's also quietly been one of the loneliest things you carry. The fact that you can see that now, and feel the weight of what it's cost you, isn't something to rush past — that's actually a meaningful moment of honesty with yourself. I'm curious, if you could let go of just a small piece of that identity — not all of it, just a little — what's the smallest, safest way you can imagine letting someone in?
